_meta: A short string given as an explicit list of Unicode code points, used to show why the number of characters a user perceives is the number of grapheme clusters, not the number of code points that len() counts, and why truncating a string by a code-point count can split a grapheme and silently mangle it. A grapheme cluster is a user-perceived character: a base code point plus any combining marks that stack on it, or an emoji built from several code points joined by zero-width joiners. Python's len() counts code points, so it overcounts the visible length of any string containing such clusters; JavaScript and Java count UTF-16 code units, overcounting even more for astral characters. Both are wrong about how many characters a person sees. The worse consequence is truncation: slicing a string to N code points to make it 'fit' can cut in the middle of a grapheme, dropping a combining accent (changing the letter) or splitting a multi-code-point emoji into a fragment. This is a separate problem from Unicode normalization (a companion module): normalizing to NFC makes canonically-equivalent strings equal, but it does not reduce every grapheme to one code point -- an emoji joined by zero-width joiners, a skin-tone-modified emoji, or a base letter with no precomposed accented form all remain several code points after NFC -- so length and truncation still need grapheme awareness that normalization does not provide. The fixture is 'Hi ' followed by a family emoji (man + zero-width joiner + woman + zero-width joiner + girl, five code points that render as one glyph) followed by '!': nine code points, five perceived characters. codepoints is the list of code point integers; note describes it. It is the fixture; the string, its code-point length, its grapheme clusters, and the two truncations are computed.
note: Hi <family emoji: man ZWJ woman ZWJ girl>!
